subject: industrial-systems
audience: FE Industrial & Systems candidates and industrial engineering students
title: The Inventory Policy That Ordered 707 Units, Not 10,000
featured_title: THE INVENTORY POLICY THAT ORDERED 707 UNITS, NOT 10000

presentation.challenge: Ordering the full annual demand once minimized ordering frequency, not total inventory cost. The EOQ was about 707 units.

practice.topic: Manufacturing, Service, and Other Production Systems
practice.primary_question: How is economic order quantity calculated from annual demand, order cost, and annual holding cost?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Ordering the entire annual demand in one batch to minimize ordering frequency while ignoring the resulting annual holding cost.

breadcrumb.name: Manufacturing, Service, and Other Production Systems

case_dna.target_misconception: The cheapest inventory policy is to order the full annual demand once because that minimizes the number of orders.
case_dna.why_plausible: Fewer orders reduce annual ordering cost, but that reasoning ignores the opposing increase in average inventory and holding cost.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: With D=10,000 units/yr, S=$50/order, and H=$2/unit-yr, EOQ=sqrt(2DS/H)=sqrt(500,000)=707.1 units. Ordering 10,000 once gives $10,000 average-inventory holding cost, far above the EOQ policy.
case_dna.corrected_model: EOQ balances annual ordering cost DS/Q against annual cycle-stock holding cost HQ/2, producing Q*=sqrt(2DS/H).

problem_statement: An item has annual demand D=10,000 units/year. Each replenishment order costs $50, and annual holding cost is $2 per unit-year. Assume constant demand, instantaneous replenishment, no shortages, and no quantity discounts. A purchasing note recommends ordering all 10,000 units once per year because that minimizes ordering frequency. Determine the economic order quantity and the annual ordering plus cycle-stock holding cost at EOQ.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: Minimizing order count did not minimize total relevant inventory cost.
gates.prompt: Which two annual costs move in opposite directions as order quantity changes?

options.label: Use Q*=sqrt(2DS/H)
options.reason: This minimizes the sum of annual ordering and cycle-stock holding costs under the stated assumptions.

options.label: Set Q=D and order once per year
options.reason: That reduces ordering cost but creates very high average inventory and holding cost.

options.label: Use Q=2DS/H without the square root
options.reason: The EOQ optimum is the square root of that ratio.

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Balance ordering and holding cost
gates.result: The economic order quantity is about 707 units.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the EOQ
gates.hint: Do not omit the square root.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: EOQ balances two opposing cost terms

cards.text: Total relevant annual cost at EOQ≈$1,414.2/year, compared with $10,050/year if 10,000 units are ordered once.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the inventory-policy note
report: C3. Therefore ordering all 10,000 units once per year minimizes inventory cost.

claims.label: C1
claims.reason: This is the stated annual demand.

claims.label: C2
claims.reason: This is the stated ordering cost.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: It considers ordering cost but ignores annual holding cost from the very large average inventory.

evidence_choices.label: Q*=sqrt(2DS/H)=707.1 units
evidence_choices.reason: This balances ordering and holding costs under the EOQ assumptions.

correction.template: The EOQ is about {eoq} units and annual ordering plus cycle-stock holding cost is about ${relevant_cost}.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Recalculate EOQ if holding cost doubles
gates.constraint: Keep D=10,000 units/year and S=$50/order, but set H=$4/unit-year.

options.label: EOQ becomes 1,000 units
options.reason: Higher holding cost reduces the optimal order quantity.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply EOQ to another item
gates.prompt: For D=4,800 units/year, S=$75/order, and H=$3/unit-year, what is EOQ?

options.label: 1,600 units
options.reason: That is not the EOQ result for the stated cost parameters.

gates.explanation: EOQ scales with the square root of demand and order cost, and inversely with the square root of holding cost.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the inventory calculation
gates.confirmation: I confirm that EOQ minimizes the tradeoff between annual ordering cost and cycle-stock holding cost under the stated deterministic assumptions.

items.label: What failed
items.value: The policy minimized the number of orders instead of total relevant inventory cost.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: Larger order quantities create larger average inventory and higher holding cost.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use Q*=sqrt(2DS/H) under the stated EOQ assumptions.

seo.seo_title: Economic Order Quantity EOQ Calculation | FE Industrial E-083
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Industrial & Systems Case E-083: with D=10,000, S=$50, and H=$2, the EOQ is about 707 units and relevant annual cost is about $1,414.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Industrial economic order quantity EOQ
seo.excerpt: Ordering once per year minimizes order count, not total inventory cost. EOQ balances ordering and holding costs.
seo.direct_answer: EOQ=sqrt(2DS/H)=sqrt[2(10,000)(50)/2]=sqrt(500,000)=707.1 units. At EOQ, annual ordering and holding costs are each about $707.1, for about $1,414.2 total relevant annual cost.

faqs.a: Q*=sqrt(2DS/H) under the standard deterministic EOQ assumptions.

faqs.q: Why not order the full annual demand once?
faqs.a: That minimizes order frequency but creates excessive average inventory and holding cost.
